name: Rafael Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can say what you'd say publicly and, separately, what you really think. Can you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive twenty minutes to Northgate Accountants, which is a firm of about twenty people in a glass box on a business park. I'm in the tax team, so it's mostly personal tax returns for landlords and self-employed people, plus VAT returns for small shops. A good day is when I find a client a legal saving they didn't know about. A bad day is three hours on the phone to the tax office on hold music.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio flat above a dry cleaner's, so my clothes always smell faintly of chemicals. The big cost is the car loan, a hundred and eighty a month, because there's no bus to the business park. I've got less than a month saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to explain a new tax rule in plain words, but I always check it against the official guidance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, which is what I've been saying for a while. At work I'd tell my manager Steve we were right not to go all in. With friends I'd say it's like the internet in the nineties: everyone shouting, then it settles down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with it, but not relaxed. My job's safe enough in that picture, but the pay at Northgate is below what city firms pay, and I've got a car loan and a month of savings. That's my worry whether AI works or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and use the AI tool a bit more for the tax rule summaries. I'd try to put a hundred a month aside once the car loan's paid off next autumn. And I'd ask Steve about the tax adviser qualification, because that's the route to better pay here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal grown-up way. Bills are bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the tax adviser qualification and what would it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the next professional exam after my accountancy one, focused only on tax. With it, I'd handle the trickier stuff, like inheritance and property sales, and I'd earn maybe fifteen percent more. Steve's said the firm might pay half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bills are bills. Which one worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, because without the car I can't get to work, and without work I can't pay the car loan. It's a stupid little circle. In AI Plateau that circle doesn't go away.

say: AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more, like the internet settling down.
Northgate was right not to **go all in** on it.
think: His job is **safe enough**, but Northgate pays below city firms.
His **car loan** and thin savings worry him whatever AI does.
do: Use the AI tool more for **tax rule summaries**.
Save **a hundred a month** once the car loan ends next autumn.
Ask Steve about funding for the **tax adviser** qualification.
feel: Uneasy in a **normal grown-up** way about bills.
S0.quote: Without the car I can't get to work, and without work I can't pay the car loan.
fieldNote: Rafael's job looks safe in this picture, but his **car loan** keeps him uneasy.
He'd use AI moderately, in line with being **steady** with new tools.
His growth plan is a **tax qualification**, not a change of field.

steps.text: Keep doing landlords' tax returns in Northgate's tax team
Save a hundred a month after the car loan ends
Ask Steve to co-fund the tax adviser exam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a manageable one, and the firms that train their people will do best. I'd post something sensible on the professional networking site, nothing dramatic. At work I'd tell the team we should learn it before it's forced on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, simple tax returns are two-thirds of my work, and that's exactly what the software would take. Steve would keep the people doing complex tax and let the rest shrink. I'm average, so it depends whether I get onto the complex side in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the tax adviser qualification this year, even if I pay for it myself in instalments. I'd get properly trained on whichever AI tool Northgate picks, because now it's clearly not going away. And I'd stop eating out and put that money towards the exam fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a race and I'm not sure I'm fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who started a year after me and does the same simple returns. Priya and I would be going for the same few complex jobs. I like Priya, which makes it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Steve said there's no room on the complex side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look in the city, which means either a longer drive or moving. A city tax firm would want the same qualification, so the exam isn't wasted either way.

say: It's a **manageable change**, and firms that **train people** will do best.
The team should learn it **before it's forced** on them.
think: Simple tax returns, **two-thirds** of his work, are exactly what it takes.
Being average, he must reach the **complex side** in time.
do: Start the **tax adviser** qualification this year, paying in instalments.
Get trained on **Northgate's AI tool** now that it's here to stay.
Stop eating out to cover the **exam fees**.
feel: Anxious, like a **race** he may not be fast enough for.
S1.quote: Simple tax returns are two-thirds of my work, and that's exactly what the software would take.
fieldNote: Rafael sees **two-thirds** of his work at risk but believes he has some control.
His rival for the safer work is **Priya**, a colleague he likes.
The **exam** is useful in both outcomes, which suits his steady approach.

steps.text: Start the tax adviser qualification, paying fees in instalments
Complete training on Northgate's chosen AI tax tool
Stop eating out to cover the exam fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from the government, quickly, and I'm not usually someone who asks for that. I'd want rules so firms phase it in rather than cutting everyone at once. I'd say it at work, calmly, because panicking in the office doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone in two years. All of it is thinking work, even the complex tax. The qualification wouldn't save me, because AGI would do inheritance tax as well as the simple stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the car and pay off the loan, then move back in with my parents in the city, where there's a bus to everywhere. I'd look for any job that's half people and half hands-on, maybe property management, because I know landlords and the buildings still need someone until the robots come. And I'd cut everything else to the bone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about how hard I studied for accountancy exams that wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say she'd been keeping my room for me, which she has. My dad would ask about my exams, and I'd have to tell him they don't count for much anymore. That conversation with my dad is the one I'd dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why property management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my clients are landlords and half their problems are boilers, leaks and tenants who don't pay. The paperwork goes to AI, but someone has to turn up and look at the damp. Robots for that come around 2031, so it's three years of breathing room.

say: The government needs a **proper plan** quickly, with firms phasing it in.
He'd say it **calmly** at work, because office panic helps no one.
think: His whole job goes **in two years**, because even complex tax is thinking work.
The **tax qualification** he studied for wouldn't save him from AGI.
do: Sell the car and **clear the loan**.
Move back in with his **parents** in the city.
Look for **property management** work with landlord clients.
feel: Alarmed, and bitter about **exams** that wouldn't matter.
S2.quote: I keep thinking about how hard I studied for accountancy exams that wouldn't matter.
fieldNote: Rafael expects to **lose his job** within two years, so alarmed fits.
He uses the **robot gap** sensibly, aiming for property work that needs someone on site.
Telling his **dad** his exams don't count is the moment he dreads.

steps.text: Sell the car and pay off the loan
Move back to his parents' place in the city
Apply for property management jobs through landlord clients
Cut all spending except phone and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and people should start now. I'd tell younger colleagues not to bet everything on accountancy exams. Online I'd share practical stuff, like which courses are worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of runway. I'd get two or three years on the complex tax side, earn a bit more, then move into something with more people and less screen before 2031. The question is just what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the tax adviser exam in the first year anyway, because it pays more now and that pay is my savings. I'd pay off the car and start putting two hundred a month away. And by year three I'd move to the city for a property or lettings job, closer to more options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the useful kind. It gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said not to bet on exams, but you'd finish yours. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd finish it because it's short-term money, not a long-term career. It's like taking a well-paid summer job before you go travelling. I'm not pretending it's the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd tell Steve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my manager Steve I'm staying three years, not thirty. Steve's a decent manager and would rather know. Maybe he'd even help me find the next thing.

say: Five years is **short but workable**, so people should start now.
Younger colleagues shouldn't bet everything on **accountancy exams**.
think: He'd get **two or three years** of better pay on complex tax.
He'd then move into **people-facing work** before 2031.
do: Finish the **tax adviser** exam in year one for the pay rise.
Clear the car and save **two hundred a month**.
Move to the city for a **lettings job** by year three.
feel: Anxious in a **useful** way that gets him moving.
S3.quote: I'd tell my manager Steve I'm staying three years, not thirty.
fieldNote: Rafael treats the exam as **short-term money**, not a career, and admits the contradiction.
He plans a **dated move** to the city, where jobs are more varied.
He still expects his **accounting job** to end, so he stays anxious.

steps.text: Finish the tax adviser exam in the first year
Pay off the car and save two hundred a month
Move to the city for a lettings job by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a sensible country to get ready. Schools, colleges, firms: everyone should be planning. I'd tell friends to treat it like any big life decision and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with time to build a second career. I could stay in tax for five or six years and move before it bites, without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northgate and finish the tax adviser exam. I'd get good with the AI tools so I'm the one checking them, not competing with them. And around 2030 I'd start looking at property management or lettings, maybe part-time first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but lower down. More like planning a move than running from a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to feel calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months' savings and a second skill. Right now I've got neither. In ten years I could get both, if I don't get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone starting accountancy today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell someone starting accountancy today to learn the tax rules and then learn people, because by 2036 the rules will be the computer's job.

say: Ten years is enough for a **sensible country** to get ready.
Friends should treat it like a **big life decision** and not panic.
think: At thirty-seven he'd have time for a **second career**.
He could stay in tax **five or six years** and move before it bites.
do: Finish the **tax adviser** exam at Northgate.
Become the team's **AI checker** rather than competing with the tools.
feel: Anxious but lower, like **planning a move** rather than fleeing a fire.
S4.quote: I'd tell someone starting accountancy today to learn the tax rules and then learn people, because by 2036 the rules will be the computer's job.
fieldNote: Rafael still expects his **current job** to go, so anxious, but with time to plan.
He names what calm would need: **three months' savings** and a second skill.
His plan mirrors other scenarios but **slower**, which suits his steady nature.

steps.text: Keep working in Northgate's tax team and finish the exam
Become the person who checks the AI's tax returns

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Everything I've studied for would be worth nothing in two years. What would help is a phase-in rule, so firms can't cut everyone at once, and grants for people who need to retrain while still paying for a car to get to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the tax office itself. If the tax office goes all AI too, I wonder who you'd call when it gets something wrong. Today calling the tax office is three hours of hold music, but at least a person answers in the end.

headlineQuote: Today calling the tax office is three hours of hold music, but at least a person answers in the end.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** in the tax team of a twenty-person firm on a business park.
He lives alone and carries a **car loan** he needs to reach work, with under a month saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and picks up tools once they're proven.
He plans in **dated steps**: a tax exam first, then property or lettings work.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, settling at anxious with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his studies would be worth **nothing** in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **phase-in rule** for firms and **retraining grants** that cover living costs.
